ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.

Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.
The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.

The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.

Equity, diversity, and inclusion are fundamental values of the American Library Association and are one of ALA’s committed key action areas which act as guiding principles for investment of energies and resources.
ALA’s Office for Diversity, Literacy and Outreach Services also encourages using a social-justice framework of diverse perspectives within LIS to advocate for equitable access to library services for all people.
In an increasingly diversifying country, library and information professionals are in need of critical thinking skills, cultural competency approaches, and new social justice approaches to executing equitable information spaces.
Currently, LIS programs, professional organizations, and LIS-based companies are competitively offering trainings around Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches to LIS.
For example, the New England Library Association (NELA) held a one-day diversity summit in the summer of 2017 with full enrollment, heavily focused on discussing race, racism, gender, sexuality, ability, immigrant and migrant rights, and social justice applications to diverse groups.

The University of North Carolina’s School of Information and Library Science offers a Diversity Advocate Certificate, the LIS press “Library Juice Press Academy” offers a course titled “Exploring and Applying Critical Theory: An Introduction for Librarians,”, and Library Journal has a number of diversity based professional development workshops such as “Diversity and Cultural Competency Training: Collections & RA,” to name a few.
This graduate track is a highly manageable 12-credit program from an accredited institution of higher education.
The proposed track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship approaches will prepare LIS graduates for diverse workplaces, serving and collaborating with diverse populations, and recruiting a more diverse workforce, as well as creating equitable information institutes.
This proposed track will be the only such track in New England and as a track, it will also serve librarians across the United States.

The Graduate Track in Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship will especially foster URI’s values of diversity, fairness and respect in students.
Information Equity, Diverse Communities, and Critical Librarianship supports URI’s mission by supporting diverse communities.
Additionally, the track will foster the leadership and critical thinking skills needed in a diversifying country and workforce.

The Department of Criminology and Criminal Justice offers a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree.
The interdisciplinary degree in Criminology and Criminal Justice provides students with a wide range of course options so that students may tailor their learning to their educational and professional interests.
Our purpose is to empower our graduates to meaningfully consider, contribute to, and reimagine discourses and decisions about crime and justice.
The CCJ Department does this by making intentional choices about our work and remaining committed to continual professional growth and community building.
The program requires 30-49 credits in the major including CCJ/SOC 230(H) (with a grade of C or better), CCJ/PSC 274(H) (with a grade of C or better), and one of three capstone classes: CCJ 403, CCJ 410 or CCJ/PSC 476.
Students must select one research methods course from the following: ECN 306, PSC 310, PSY 200, or SOC 301.

Students are required to take six elective courses selected from the following two areas: criminology electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 334, 370, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 450, 476; AAF/HIS 366; PHL 318; PSY 254, 466; SOC 420; criminal justice electives – AAF 230; CCJ 200 (approved topics), 280, 285, 290,,, 332, 333, 381 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class), 456, 480, 490, 400 (approved topics), 403, 410, 476; CHM 391 (must either be repeated 3 times or taken in combination with CCJ 381 and/or ITR 305 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class); CCJ/HIS 361, AAF/HIS 366; ITR 305 (must be taken in combination with CHM 391 and/or CCJ 381 for a total of 3 credits to count as 1 elective class) PSC 334, 371, 388, 472; PSY 465; SOC 303.
At least two courses must be taken from each elective area and no more than four courses can be taken in either area.
All electives must be a minimum of 3 credits.
While CCJ 403, 410, and CCJ/PSC 476 are each capstone classes and electives, students may not use the same course to count as both a capstone and an elective class.

When appropriate, and by permission of the Department Chair, students may substitute internship credit (SOC 477, PSC 375/376, PSY 305, or GWS 300) or independent study credit (CCJ 485, SOC 498/499, PSC 455/456, PSY 489, or GWS 450) for one of their elective courses listed above.
No more than 3 credits may be used toward the major from internship or independent study.
Internal transfers into the CCJ major form a different major, or students wishing to add the CCJ major to their current major, must have a minimum 2.50 GPA.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
At least 30 of these credits must be in courses at the 300-level or above.
In order to transfer into the criminology and criminal justice B.A. program from University College for Academic Success, a student must have completed at least 24 credits and have an earned a minimum of a 2.0 GPA.
